## 1. Problem Statement and Background

### Problem Definition

1.1 The central focus of this dataset is to provide insights into the factors influencing peoples' willingness to consider purchasing an electric vehicle (EV). In particular, this dataset includes factors ranging from peoples' age, income, and daily commute to their range anxiety level, environmental concern level, and whether or not a subsidy is available.   

1.2 The target audience may include any of the following:

* Automotive Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs): OEMs have a vested interest in consumer behavior and trends in
particular automotive subgroups. Electric vehicles are growing in popularity and charging stations are becoming more prevalent across the United States. This information may assist OEMs in determining the amount of resources they divert towards an electric fleet.

* Local City Governments: Public charging stations require investment and planning from government. This data and analysis may assist in determining to what degree charging stations should be prioritized for the benefit of their citizens. 

* Electric Utilities: Power companies would benefit from knowing how prevalent EVs are and how much they're influenced by local charging stations. If charging stations increased, there may be a change in peoples' willingness to buy EVs, and thus increase usage on these stations.  


1.3 Related Work: Prediction of Electic Vehicle (EV) sales is a big topic today. There are many approaches being used. In one study we found, researchers from National Pingtung University in Taiwan used Machine Learning to predict trends of EV sales on a macro scale. They talk about how machine learning has replaced more traditional linear regression or similar models. They also heavily considered the environmental impact of a large portion of the population switching to EVs. An article by Bloomberg addressed the trending topic of the proportion of EV ownership by country. These trends can tell manufacturers which countries to focus on. Many automotive manufacturers also run their own studies to help determine the viability of EV production. Most of these studies are focused on global or national trends. However, our project is focused on the prediction of whether individuals will purchase an EV or not. 

(Citations: https://www.sciencedirect.com/org/science/article/pii/S1062737523000574#secd5e912, https://about.bnef.com/insights/clean-transport/electric-vehicle-outlook/)


1.4 For measuring accuracy, since there is a large class imbalance (approximately 82.5% with 0 on Will_Buy_EV), a naive model assuming 0 for all data points would yield an 82.5% accuracy. So, accuracy will be a poor measure of success. Thus, measuring success will be done with the following:  

* AOC/ROC: Measuring a model's discriminatory power.

* Precision, Recall, and F1 Score: Ensuring the model minimizes false positives and false negatives.

* AIC/BIC: Comparing model performance across all four models used.

## 2. Data and Exploratory Analysis

2.1 The dataset includes 15 features, including numerical, categorical, and character data types. The target feature is "Will_Buy_EV" which states whether an individual will express interest in buying an EV (0 for no, 1 for yes). The data is based on a real world situation but is synthetically-generated. 


Summary of Features: 

| Feature | Data Type |
| :----------------------: | :------------------: |
| **ID** | Integer |
| **Age** | Integer |
| **Annual Income USD** | Double |
| **Daily Commute (km)** | Double |
| **Number of Cars Owned** | Integer | 
| **Charging Stations Near Home** | Integer |
| **Charging Stations Near Work** | Integer |
| **Environmental Concern Level** | Double |
| **Gender** | Character |
| **City Type** | Character |
| **Current Car Type** | Character |
| **Home Charging Possible** | Character |
| **Subsidy Available** | Character |
| **Range Anxiety Level** | Character |
| **Will Buy EV** | Integer |

Looking at the structure of classes in the training dataset, 82.54% of individuals indicated no intent to purchase an EV, while 18.46% indicated an intent to purchase an EV.

2.2 Since this was a synthetically-generated dataset, there were no missing data points in any of the rows. The only transformation was to convert the target variable to a factor for plotting purposes. We found outliers for most of the numerical features, but given the large dataset, we decided not to remove any instances. 

2.3 The packages used so far are dplyr and tidymodels. dplyr is being used for the arrange() function to sort columns. tidymodels is used to generate training, validation, and test sets.




```{r setup, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}


suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr)) #arrange func
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidymodels)) #training/test split
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(janitor)) #make_clean_names/clean_names() if needed

train_data <- read.csv("train.csv")
sum(!complete.cases(train_data))
#0 rows including missing data


train_data <- read.csv("train.csv") |>
  na.omit()

variables <- names(train_data)
variables <- variables[-15]
variables <- variables[-1]


set.seed(42)
data_split <- initial_split(train_data, prop=0.70)
train_data <- training(data_split)
test_val_data <- testing(data_split)

data_split2 <- initial_split(test_val_data, prop=0.5)
val_data <- training(data_split2)
test_data <- testing(data_split2)


train_data$Will_Buy_EV <- ifelse(train_data$Will_Buy_EV == "Yes", 1, 0)
train_data$Will_Buy_EV <- as.factor(train_data$Will_Buy_EV)

test_data$Will_Buy_EV <- ifelse(test_data$Will_Buy_EV == "Yes", 1, 0)
test_data$Will_Buy_EV <- as.factor(test_data$Will_Buy_EV)

val_data$Will_Buy_EV <- ifelse(val_data$Will_Buy_EV == "Yes", 1, 0)
val_data$Will_Buy_EV <- as.factor(val_data$Will_Buy_EV)


summary(train_data$Will_Buy_EV)
sapply(train_data, typeof)

```{r Variable Selection, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
report <- data.frame(Independent_Variable = character(), 
                     Correlation = numeric())
options(scipen = 999)
for (var in variables) {
  if(is.numeric(train_data[[var]])){
    cors <- cor(train_data[[var]], as.numeric(train_data$Will_Buy_EV))
    #print(paste0("Correlation between ", var, " and target: ", round(cors, 5)))
    new_report <- data.frame(Independent_Variable = var,
                             Correlation = cors)
    report <- rbind(new_report, report)
  }
}

report <- report |>
  arrange(desc(abs(Correlation)))

report
```


## Exploratory Plots for Numerical Features

```{r Pie Chart Will_Buy_EV, fig.cap="The pie chart shows the percentage of individuals with expressed interest in purchasing an EV.", fig.align="center", echo=TRUE}

counts <- table(train_data$Will_Buy_EV)
percentages <- round(prop.table(counts) * 100, 1)

pie(table(train_data$Will_Buy_EV), main = "Proportion of EV Purchase Interest",
  labels = paste0(c("No (0)", "Yes (1)"), ": " , percentages, "%"), col = c("red", "green")
)
```


```{r Will_Buy_EV vs ECL, fig.cap="The plot above appears to show a positive correlation between environmental concern level and one's willingness to buy an EV. ```{r Exploratory Modeling, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
model1 <- glm(reformulate(variables, response="Will_Buy_EV"), data=train_data, family=binomial(link="logit")) 


ggplot(train_data, aes(x = Environmental_Concern_Level, y = as.numeric(as.character(Will_Buy_EV)))) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family=binomial(link="logit")),
              formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE) +
  ylim(0,1)

ggplot(train_data, aes(x = Annual_Income_USD, y = as.numeric(as.character(Will_Buy_EV)))) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family=binomial(link="logit")),
              formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE) +
  ylim(0,1)
```

```{r Predictions, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
#hold all variables constant - copy first row 100 times
new_data <- train_data[rep(1,100), ]

#evenly space out values for ECL across the 100 rows
new_data$Environmental_Concern_Level <- seq(
  min(train_data$Environmental_Concern_Level),
  max(train_data$Environmental_Concern_Level),
  length.out = 100
)

#produce a prediction feature
new_data$probability <- predict(model1, newdata = new_data, type="response")

#plot ECL vs predictions to see trend
ggplot(new_data, aes(x = Environmental_Concern_Level, y = probability)) +
  geom_line() + 
  labs(x = "Environmental Concern Level", y = "Predicted Probability of Buying an EV") +
  ylim(0,1)
```




### EDA Conclusions:
Due to this being a synthetically generated data set, there are some weird behaviors with some of the features. Age appears to be uniformly distributed which does not match real world age distribution. We hypothesized that charging station availability would have a stronger correlation, but our initial graphs seem to show that almost no correlation exists with whether or not an individual will buy an EV. Based on our exploratory plots we think that Environmental Concern Level and Annual Income will be the best linear predictors for willingness to make an EV purchase.
